text: You've built the identity fabric, the segmentation, the assume-breach containment, and a way to measure maturity. None of that tells you what to build first in year one versus year three. This lesson is about sequencing — turning a list of good zero trust ideas into a roadmap that survives real budget cycles and more than one CISO.

A workable rollout sorts work into three horizons. Quick wins, in roughly the first six months, reduce real risk without a multi-year project underneath them — MFA everywhere, tightening standing admin roles, turning on conditional access the tenant already licenses. Foundational work, months six through eighteen, is slower and mostly invisible: this is where identity becomes the real control plane and segmentation replaces the flat network. Long-haul initiatives — workload identity, API-level zero trust, SaaS posture management — only make sense once that foundation is load-bearing.

Order isn't arbitrary, because the horizons depend on each other. Micro-segmentation is close to meaningless without the identity signals feeding its policy decisions — you can't make a segment-level access decision on device compliance if that signal doesn't exist yet. Data and API-level controls assume segmentation is already there to contain a failure. And maturity scoring measures nothing real if it's scoring a foundation that was never built. Identity leads, segmentation follows identity, and everything else follows segmentation.

A real roadmap line names three things: which horizon the initiative belongs to, which earlier initiative it depends on, and what specifically changes for users and attackers once it ships. Not 'implement conditional access' — 'standing admin access to production is gone, elevation expires in four hours.' That specificity is what separates a roadmap from a wish list, and it's what the rest of this chapter will hold every initiative to.

Next lesson assumes you can't fund or staff every one of these horizons at once, which is true for almost every real program, and builds the prioritization framework for deciding what gets fixed first when resources are limited: highest risk, weighed against what's actually feasible to ship right now.
